Read 01 to 12, left to right. Start with the picture. Use TLS-GUIDE.md for the full explanation.
Client = asks. Server = answers. Both are programs on our Kali machine.
lo = local loopback path. A port is a numbered door: 8443 for TLS 1.3, 8444 for TLS
1.2. No Wi-Fi or external target is involved.

A key is numerical data. Encrypt = scramble. Decrypt = recover with the right key.
AES-GCM protects the request and file.
Each direction has its own key.
RSA: public key checks a signature
Recovering the factors from a very large product is hard. Real RSA uses large numbers
and padding. This toy example is not secure.
A signature is a checkable seal on exact data. It does not hide that data. The CA
signs an ID. In TLS 1.3, the server signs the setup conversation.

RSA = Rivest, Shamir, Adleman. rsa:2048 = a 2048-bit RSA key pair.

CSR = Certificate Signing Request. It asks for a certificate. It contains no private key.
The signed certificate contains the public key, names, dates and CA signature.
SAY IT Making an ID card is different from opening a secure connection.
Command meanings: -newkey makes a pair. -x509 makes a certificate. -CAkey signs.
CA = certificate authority, a trusted certificate issuer. Trust must start somewhere.
GENERAL CHAIN: each issuer signs the next certificate
Trust store = the client's chosen list of trusted issuers. --cacert ca.crt supplies our CA
to curl. -CAfile supplies it to OpenSSL. Self-signing alone creates no trust.
Client checks: signature path to a trusted CA, permitted use, name and dates. SAN =
allowed names on the ID. The live server must also prove it holds the matching
SAY IT The CA signs the name-to-key link. The server proves it owns that key.
A valid certificate checks a named endpoint. It does not promise an honest website.
Handshake = agree on methods and secrets, then check who is answering.

mathematics and temporary private inputs, not paint.

Evidence: t_tls12 and t_tls13. Full suitable handshake + matching RSA key are required.
Capturing packets records bytes. Decrypting them also requires suitable secret material.
Our server's -keylogfile exports connection secrets. Wireshark can then calculate the
data keys. This is endpoint-assisted decryption, not a break from packets alone.
tls13-with-keys.pcapng = copy with secrets inside. It opens decrypted. Clear Wireshark
secrets or use separate profiles for comparisons.
SAY IT The key log supplies exactly what the ordinary observer is missing.
Evidence: existing t_tls13 and t_tls12 decryption checks.
The fake server: refusal is success
Fake server on port 9443. Same name, localhost. Different self-signed certificate.
Client trusts Lab CA -> fake ID has no path to it -> curl error 60 -> HTTP witness is
not sent. TLS setup bytes still reach the fake server.
Client skips the ID check -> encrypts for the fake server -> fake server decrypts its
own incoming request -> witness appears in its log.
Anyone can print localhost on a
A thief can open a box you locked for
Why the timeout? The fake server logs the POST but sends no normal HTTP reply. The
two-second timeout does not prove delivery failed. The server log proves the witness
SAY IT TLS protected the delivery to the wrong recipient after we disabled its identity
Evidence: t_fake. Direct fake-server test, not a transparent man-in-the-middle interception.
